paragraphs.title: The Devastation of the Earth and the Equalization of All Classes

answers: He makes it empty and waste
easy.explanation: Isaiah 24:1 says, “the Lord maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste.”
easy.q: What does the Lord do to the earth at the beginning of the passage?

easy.explanation: The verse says that the Lord “scattereth abroad the inhabitants thereof.”
easy.q: What happens to the inhabitants of the earth?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes the earth being emptied, ruined, and made desolate.
medium.q: What does “maketh it waste” mean in this passage?

answers: The people, priest, servant, master, buyer, and seller are treated alike
medium.explanation: The verse repeatedly says, “as with” one class, “so with” another.
medium.q: How are the social classes compared in verse 2?

answers: Because the city gates were closed
Because its inhabitants transgressed the laws and broke the covenant
medium.explanation: The inhabitants “have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant.”
medium.q: Why is the earth defiled and punished?

answers: The judgment removes ordinary social distinctions
The judgment separates servants from masters
challenge.explanation: The passage presents every social class as sharing the same judgment and condition.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between the equal treatment of the classes and the judgment?

answers: That the situation is only temporary
That the destruction affects the whole land and its people
That only one city is affected
challenge.explanation: The repeated language shows that the judgment is widespread and comprehensive.
challenge.q: What do the repeated descriptions of emptiness, spoil, and mourning emphasize?

answers: Breaking the covenant, judgment on the earth, and few survivors
Building the city, drinking wine, and singing
challenge.explanation: The passage connects disobedience with judgment and the survival of only a few.
challenge.q: Which sequence of ideas appears in these verses?

paragraphs.title: The Disappearance of Joy and the Ruin of the City

answers: They are sent to another city
easy.explanation: Isaiah says, “The new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth.”
easy.q: What happens to the new wine and the vine?

easy.explanation: The mirth of tabrets, the noise of rejoicing, and the joy of the harp cease.

answers: Broken down, desolate, and shut up
easy.explanation: The city is called “the city of confusion,” and every house is shut up.

medium.explanation: “Ceaseth” means comes to an end or stops.

answers: It has become empty and desolate
It has become safe and festive
medium.explanation: Every house is shut so that no one may come in, showing the city’s desolation.
medium.q: What does the shutting of every house show about the city?

medium.explanation: The streets contain “a crying for wine,” while the joy of the land is gone.
medium.q: What replaces joy in the streets?

answers: Their loss emphasizes the disappearance of social joy
They prove that the city is flourishing
challenge.explanation: Their mourning and cessation symbolize the loss of celebration and ordinary community life.
challenge.q: How do wine, music, and the vine contribute to the description of judgment?

answers: It moves from music and joy to emptiness, crying, and ruin
It moves from crying to celebration and victory
It moves from a closed city to a rebuilt city
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts former rejoicing with the city’s desolation and destruction.
challenge.q: What change takes place within the passage?

answers: Joy has disappeared from the land
Joy has moved to another city
challenge.explanation: The statement means that joy is extinguished throughout the land.
challenge.q: What does “all joy is darkened” mean in context?

paragraphs.title: The Remnant and the Song from the Ends of the Earth

answers: Olives and grapes left after the harvest
easy.explanation: The remnant is compared to the shaking of an olive tree and gleaning grapes after vintage.
easy.q: What is the remnant compared to?

answers: They lift up their voice and sing
They only flee from the city
easy.explanation: The passage says, “They shall lift up their voice, they shall sing.”
easy.q: What do the remaining people do?

easy.explanation: The people sing “for the majesty of the Lord” and glorify His name.

answers: Grapes left after the main harvest
medium.explanation: Gleaning grapes are the few grapes remaining after the vintage is finished.

answers: A small remnant on earth and songs heard from distant places
A large city and a small village
medium.explanation: The passage describes a small remnant while songs come from the uttermost parts of the earth.
medium.q: What central contrast appears in the passage?

medium.explanation: They are commanded, “glorify ye the Lord,” including the name of the Lord God of Israel.
medium.q: What are people in the fires and isles of the sea told to do?

answers: A small remnant remains after widespread destruction
The land has become more fertile
challenge.explanation: The comparison emphasizes how few remain after the judgment.
challenge.q: What does the comparison to gleaned grapes and olives symbolize?

answers: The song erases all mention of betrayal
Praise is heard while betrayal and distress still remain
The song is heard only in the ruined city
challenge.explanation: Songs of glory are heard, but the prophet also cries of treacherous dealing and personal anguish.
challenge.q: How does the song relate to the condition of the world?

answers: The songs come from distant places
The songs come only from Jerusalem
The songs are heard inside a closed house
challenge.explanation: The phrase indicates the farthest or most remote parts of the earth.
challenge.q: What does “from the uttermost part of the earth” suggest?

paragraphs.title: Fear, Traps, and the Shaking Earth

answers: Fear, the pit, and the snare
Wine, the vine, and the harp
The law, the ordinance, and the covenant
easy.explanation: The verse says, “Fear, and the pit, and the snare, are upon thee.”
easy.q: Which three dangers are named together in verse 17?

easy.explanation: The person who flees from fear “shall fall into the pit.”
easy.q: What happens to the person who flees from the noise of fear?

easy.explanation: The earth is utterly broken down, clean dissolved, moved exceedingly, and reels to and fro.
easy.q: How is the earth described at the end of the passage?

medium.explanation: A snare is a device or trap used to catch someone.
medium.q: What is a “snare” in this passage?

answers: The one fleeing from fear falls into the pit, and the one leaving the pit is caught in the snare
medium.explanation: Each attempted escape leads directly to another danger.
medium.q: Why is there no escape from danger?

answers: The windows from on high being opened
medium.explanation: The verse says, “the windows from on high are open, and the foundations of the earth do shake.”
medium.q: What does the passage say causes the foundations of the earth to shake?

answers: Many dangers leave no safe direction
A change from fear to joy
challenge.explanation: The sequence presents danger surrounding the inhabitant on every side.
challenge.q: What does the sequence “fear, the pit, and the snare” emphasize?

answers: Its transgression lies heavily upon it and contributes to its fall
challenge.explanation: The earth’s transgression is described as heavy upon it before it falls.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between the earth’s transgression and its fall?

answers: The passage moves from personal danger to the shaking and collapse of the whole earth
The earth’s collapse is followed by the rebuilding of the city
The passage moves from joy to drinking wine
challenge.explanation: The verses begin with traps for individuals and end with the earth reeling and falling.
challenge.q: What development occurs from verses 18 through 20?

paragraphs.title: Judgment on Heaven and Earth and God’s Reign in Zion

answers: Only the inhabitants of one city
The host of the high ones and the kings of the earth
easy.explanation: The Lord will punish “the host of the high ones” and “the kings of the earth.”

answers: They are gathered and shut up as prisoners
easy.explanation: They are gathered as prisoners, shut up in prison, and later visited.

answers: Only in the isles of the sea
easy.explanation: The Lord of hosts will reign “in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem.”
easy.q: Where does the passage say that the Lord will reign?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to the high or heavenly host mentioned alongside the kings of the earth.
medium.q: What does “the host of the high ones” refer to?

answers: They are visited or brought into judgment
medium.explanation: The passage says that “after many days shall they be visited.”
medium.q: What happens to the prisoners after many days?

answers: The moon is confounded and the sun is ashamed
They disappear from the heavens completely
medium.explanation: Isaiah says, “the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed.”
medium.q: What happens to the moon and the sun before the Lord’s reign?

answers: Judgment on earthly rulers places God’s supreme reign above them
The kings become partners in God’s reign
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from the confinement of earthly rulers to the glorious reign of the Lord.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between judgment on the kings and God’s reign in Zion?

answers: The superiority of the Lord’s glory over the heavenly lights
The return of joy to the city
The victory of the earthly kings
challenge.explanation: The sun and moon appear diminished in comparison with the glory of the Lord.
challenge.q: What does the shame of the sun and confusion of the moon express?

challenge.explanation: The final words say that the Lord will reign gloriously “before his ancients.”
challenge.q: Before whom is the Lord’s glory revealed at the end?
